what-is-school-readiness:
School readiness is mostly not academic. That is the whole of it, and almost everything sold to parents under this heading is aimed at the smallest part.

A child arriving at school able to read but unable to ask for help, wait, or recover from a small setback will have a harder term than one who arrives with none of the letters and all of the rest.

What schools actually notice

Ask a reception teacher what makes a child's first term go well and the answers are consistent, and none of them are academic.

  • Can they separate from you. Not without any distress, but recoverably.
  • Can they ask for what they need. The toilet, help with a zip, a drink. A child who cannot ask has a very long day.
  • Can they manage themselves physically. Coat, shoes, toilet, lunch. Independence here buys enormous confidence.
  • Can they wait a little. For a turn, for attention, for the end of something.
  • Can they recover. From a fall, a lost game, a friend who said no. Not without upset, but back within a few minutes.
  • Can they attend to an adult in a group. Ten minutes of a story with other children around.

The academic part, honestly

Useful: recognising their own name, holding a pencil comfortably, hearing rhyme and initial sounds, counting real objects, knowing some letter sounds.

Not useful: reading before starting, writing sentences, knowing all twenty-six letter names, worksheets. None of these predict how the year goes, and a child pushed to them at four often arrives with the thing that does matter, willingness, already dented.

What to do with the year before

Practise the independence, because it is the part that is genuinely learnable in a year. Let them dress themselves even when it is slower. Let them carry their own bag, open their own packet, put on their own shoes.

Talk more than you teach. Read aloud daily. Play with sounds in the car. Let them play with other children without you refereeing every dispute.

And practise the small separations: an afternoon with a grandparent, a session somewhere without you. Recovering from a goodbye is a skill, and it is better rehearsed before the day it matters.

The uncomfortable bit about age

Within any school year the oldest and youngest children can be nearly twelve months apart, which at four is a quarter of a lifetime. The younger ones are more often identified as struggling, and the effect is measurable for several years before it fades.

Worth knowing, because it means a summer-born child finding the first year hard is very often not behind at all. They are younger, and it will even out.

Readiness is not a set of things a child knows. It is whether they can manage a day among other people without you, and it is built by being allowed to do things themselves.
child-development-by-age-a-parents-guide:
A map of the whole of childhood, stage by stage. Every age here is the middle of a wide range, and a child a year either side of any of it is inside the ordinary spread.

StageWhat is being builtWhat is normal and looks alarmingWhat helps most
2 to 4 Language, the body, and the arrival of a separate will Tantrums, refusal, no sharing, extreme reactions to small things Talking constantly, a calm adult, room to move
4 to 6 Imagination, sound awareness, first self-control, first friendships Self-control that vanishes when tired, intense fairness applied selectively Read-aloud, sound play, unstructured play with other children
6 to 8 Reading fluency, concrete logic, competence as identity Losing badly, forgetting instructions, comparing themselves constantly Volume of easy reading, real responsibility, specific noticing
8 to 11 Independent thinking, sustained attention, working without an adult Strong opinions, questioning rules, wanting privacy Things they can own, hard problems with somebody nearby
11 to 14 Identity, belonging, judgement, self-mastery Friends outranking family, mood swings, apparent loss of interest in everything Staying in the room, real responsibility, sleep
14 to 16 Discernment, authorship, purpose, readiness to leave Risk-taking, arguing well, withdrawing then reappearing Being treated as competent, and a door that stays open

Three things the table cannot show

The tracks run at different speeds in the same child. Language, movement, social understanding and self-control each have their own timetable. A child ahead on one is frequently behind on another, and neither is a trade for the other.

Nothing arrives finished. Self-control appears at four and is still maturing at twenty-four. Reading arrives at six and is still developing at sixteen through vocabulary and knowledge. A capacity showing up is the start of it, not the end.

Regression is normal. Children commonly go backwards for a few weeks before or during a leap, and again around any upheaval: a new sibling, a move, a change of school. A skill that wobbles is usually a skill being rebuilt at a higher level.

When to ask somebody

Not for a single late milestone. Worth raising: several areas behind at once, a skill lost rather than not yet gained, no interest in other people, or a persistent unease of your own that has lasted months rather than weeks.

That last one is not a lesser reason. Parents are usually right that something is different even when they are wrong about what it is.

This piece is general guidance and is not a substitute for an assessment by someone who knows your child.
